question: Where do T-cells complete their maturation before entering circulation?
explanation: Both cell types start as stem cells in the bone marrow, but T-cells travel specifically to the thymus to mature fully. [learn more](BMP111_U6_T6#BMP111_U6_T6_h1)

question: What main feature sets adaptive immunity apart from innate immunity?
explanation: Adaptive immunity tailors its defense to target specific foreign antigens rather than mounting a generalized response. [learn more](BMP111_U6_T6#BMP111_U6_T6_h1)

question: What is the main job of antigen-presenting cells in the immune system?

options.C: Display antigen fragments on MHC molecules
options.D: Secrete thick mucus barriers in the lungs

explanation: These cells capture pathogens and show pieces of them to T-cells using specialized surface proteins. [learn more](BMP111_U6_T6#BMP111_U6_T6_h2)

question: Why does the body go through clonal selection during an infection?

options.A: To flush out toxins through the urinary system
options.B: To multiply the specific lymphocytes that match the invader
options.C: To destroy healthy tissue to prevent pathogen spread
options.D: To shut down the immune response safely

explanation: Clonal selection makes many copies of the exact cell needed to fight the specific germ present in the body. [learn more](BMP111_U6_T6#BMP111_U6_T6_h2)

question: Which cells are responsible for mass-producing antibodies during a humoral response?
explanation: Activated B-cells transform into plasma cells, which function as dedicated antibody factories. [learn more](BMP111_U6_T6#BMP111_U6_T6_h3)

question: Where do humoral immune responses mainly carry out their work?
explanation: The term humoral refers to body fluids like blood and lymph where circulating antibodies neutralize floating pathogens. [learn more](BMP111_U6_T6#BMP111_U6_T6_h3)

question: Which antibody class is found in breast milk and protects mucosal surfaces?
explanation: Secretory IgA is abundant in breast milk, saliva, and tears, defending mucous membranes against invading pathogens. [learn more](BMP111_U6_T6#BMP111_U6_T6_h4)

question: A newborn receives temporary immunity across the placenta from the mother. Which antibody provides this?
explanation: IgG is the only antibody class small and specialized enough to cross the human placenta from mother to fetus. [learn more](BMP111_U6_T6#BMP111_U6_T6_h4)

question: When is the cell-mediated immune response primarily called into action?

options.A: When bacteria float freely in the blood plasma
options.B: When large parasites attach to the skin surface
options.C: When simple chemical toxins dissolve in body fluids
options.D: When host cells are infected by intracellular pathogens

explanation: Cell-mediated immunity is specifically designed to handle viruses and other invaders hiding inside body cells. [learn more](BMP111_U6_T6#BMP111_U6_T6_h5)

question: What is NOT a feature of standard T-cell activation and response?

options.A: Requirement for antigens to be presented on MHC molecules
options.B: Induction of apoptosis in targeted rogue cells
options.C: Direct interaction with infected or abnormal host cells
options.D: Secretion of free-floating antibodies into blood plasma

explanation: Antibody secretion is the job of B-cells and plasma cells in humoral immunity, not T-cells. [learn more](BMP111_U6_T6#BMP111_U6_T6_h5)

question: Which surface marker protein is found on Helper T-cells?
explanation: Helper T-cells bear the CD4 protein on their surface, making them the primary target for the human immunodeficiency virus. [learn more](BMP111_U6_T6#BMP111_U6_T6_h6)

question: What is the primary role of Cytotoxic T-cells during an immune response?

options.A: Produce large quantities of circulating antibodies
options.B: Directly destroy virus-infected and cancerous body cells
options.C: Coordinate immune cell communication via cytokines
options.D: Swallow up debris through phagocytic action

explanation: CD8-positive cytotoxic T-cells seek out abnormal or infected host cells and trigger their destruction. [learn more](BMP111_U6_T6#BMP111_U6_T6_h6)

question: Why is a secondary immune response so much faster than a primary response?

options.A: Pre-existing memory cells instantly recognize and react to the antigen
options.B: Bone marrow creates brand new white blood cells instantly
options.C: The pathogen becomes weaker every time it enters the human body
options.D: Innate barriers disappear completely after the first infection occurs

explanation: Memory cells left over from the first exposure allow the immune system to skip the slow initial activation steps. [learn more](BMP111_U6_T6#BMP111_U6_T6_h7)

question: What is a key feature of a primary immune response to a new pathogen?

options.A: It clears the foreign microbe within a few hours
options.B: It relies exclusively on circulating maternal antibodies
options.C: It prevents all future infections from occurring
options.D: It is slow and usually accompanied by clinical illness

explanation: Because the body has no prior experience with the germ, it takes time to build a defense, leading to sickness. [learn more](BMP111_U6_T6#BMP111_U6_T6_h7)

question: How do vaccines safely protect a patient from future infectious diseases?

options.A: By stimulating a primary response to create lasting memory cells
options.B: By permanently blocking all foreign antigen recognition
options.C: By providing permanent passive immunity using animal antibodies
options.D: By destroying the patient's existing white blood cells

explanation: Vaccines introduce safe antigens so the body builds memory cells without suffering the full disease. [learn more](BMP111_U6_T6#BMP111_U6_T6_h8)

question: Which antibody class is primarily responsible for triggering allergic reactions?
explanation: IgE antibodies bind to mast cells and basophils, releasing chemicals that cause allergic and inflammatory reactions. [learn more](BMP111_U6_T6#BMP111_U6_T6_h8)
